title: Cult of the Lamb: studio-published follower reaction

people.name: Jan F Sorrentino
people.role: Animator at Massive Monster; maker of Doom & Shroom fan-animation

summary: A studio-posted rabbit follower reaction separates a strongly readable eye design from a changing small mouth.

observations.text: Two inspected frames show the rabbit with very large dark oval eyes and thin pale vertical pupils. Its mouth changes from a small tooth-bearing shape to an open smile while its hands stay near its chest.
In the second inspected frame, a foreground finger points toward the rabbit. This grounds the reaction in an interaction, although isolated screenshots do not establish the precise sequence or cause.

mistIdeas: Our inference: use a stable, recognizable eye design with a small number of clear mouth changes so talking does not erase the face's identity.
Our inference: attach reactions to a visible or audible event and give attention a target. Do not copy the follower's extreme eye proportions into every MIST state.

title: Webbed: greeting and dance as social expression

people.name: Riley Neville
people.role: Programming, Art, Sound and Game Design

summary: A tiny spider remains socially readable through visible eyes, orientation and raised front limbs; the developer provides original greeting and dance GIFs.

observations.text: In the greeting GIF's inspected frame, the spider sits directly beside another insect under its speech balloon. The small bright eye marks remain visible against the dark face, while proximity makes the interaction legible.
The dance GIF's inspected frame shows the spider leaning with front limbs raised beside a much larger moth. The face occupies very little of the image; the limb silhouette supplies a stronger signal.
Neville describes the spider's dance as a wiggle-arms move and discusses procedurally animated characters in the GameMaker interview.

mistIdeas: Our inference: make a greeting a brief acknowledgement of the arriving person, with a held look and one small gesture. The social target matters more than adding a large smile.
Our inference: test MIST reactions at the smallest intended display size. If the face becomes hard to read, reinforce the same intent through a body tilt rather than adding tiny facial detail.
Our inference: reserve an energetic celebration for meaningful success; return to a settled attentive pose after it.

title: Pikuniku: two eyes, posture and comic context
summary: A useful limit case: a character can remain readable with two eye dots and little facial detail when its posture carries the action.

observations.text: The official swimming screenshot shows the red character tilted diagonally with bent legs and two small eye dots; no mouth is visible in this pose. Orientation and limb silhouette supply most of the action information.
De Bock explicitly says the minimal aesthetic was chosen to keep attention on characters' physical appearance and body language.

mistIdeas: Our inference: test an attentive MIST state with a quiet mouth and a deliberate eye/face orientation change, so the display can communicate without constant mouth activity.
Our inference: assign a single posture-like change to each event: lean or shift toward input, compress on uncertainty, return on acknowledgement.
Our inference: compare an eyes-only reaction against a full facial reaction at small size; keep the simpler version if it reads equally well.

title: Lil Gator Game: a heavy head with a simple face

people.name: Scott Slucher
people.role: Developer explaining his character design and animation implementation

summary: Slucher's own explanation separates authored movement, speed-dependent blending, head lag and secondary physics.

observations.text: The inspected sword-swing image puts the large pale eye and black pupil against the green head; the open jaw and broad head silhouette remain readable amid the flying cardboard. This is a still-image observation.
Slucher says the oversized head and arms make small movements read strongly; he accounts for the head's weight when animating.

Slucher describes blend trees driven by speed and surface angle, then procedural head lag and body leaning in turns. He explicitly says the blended animations are subtler, so large movements are not constant.

mistIdeas: Our inference: give MIST's eye/head orientation a small follow-through relative to a body turn, then let it settle cleanly.
Our inference: distinguish a quiet attention shift from a full-body enthusiastic response; do not reuse the same large bounce for both.
Our inference: test the expression in a frozen silhouette first. The face should remain readable before adding spring motion.

title: BattleBlock Theater: simple faces with authored puppet movement

people.name: Derek Lieu
people.role: Cutscene animator for the nine shipped game cutscenes

people.name: Dan Paladin
people.role: Art, storyboards and rough opening animatic; art and animation for the 2011 opening/prologue

summary: The closest structural lesson for MIST: an extremely simple face can act through the movement of the whole graphic and carefully chosen reaction shapes.

observations.text: The official finished cutscene still uses tiny eyes and large open mouths on white, flat characters. Round, square and irregular heads remain readable against a busy purple scene.

Lieu describes sketching puppet motion paths, manually keyframing rotation and offsetting Hatty from the boat movement to avoid rigid attachment. He also describes adjustable inertial overshoot and settling.
The production began with Paladin's rough drawings and story beats, which Lieu animated before swapping in final artwork. This is evidence for testing acting before surface polish.

mistIdeas: Our inference: validate MIST reactions as rough eye-and-mouth poses before adding glow, noise or shading.
Our inference: offset eye arrival, mouth arrival and whole-face settle slightly so a reaction does not resemble one rigid layer being scaled.
Our inference: try a small rotation or translation overshoot followed by a deliberate readable hold. Tune recovery to the event's importance; avoid making every idle movement bounce.
Our inference: preserve simple facial marks and spend the motion budget on clear staging, gaze direction and purposeful pauses.
